title: Boeuf Bourguignon
subtitle: Beef braised slowly in Burgundy wine with lardons, mushrooms, and pearl onions
excerpt: Chunks of beef braised for three hours in a full bottle of red Burgundy until the meat is falling apart and the sauce is thick, glossy, and deeply savoury. The classic French braise.

recipe.sourceNotes: Boeuf bourguignon is a braise from the Burgundy region of France, historically made to tenderise the tough working oxen of the area using the region's most celebrated product: its wine. The dish was a peasant preparation long before Julia Child popularised it in English-speaking kitchens through her 1961 book Mastering the Art of French Cooking. Child's version, faithful to the Burgundian tradition, specifies: browning the beef in batches to avoid steaming, marinating in wine (optional but traditional), braising in the oven rather than on the hob for even heat, and adding the mushrooms and onions separately so each element keeps its character. The dish is always better the next day: it should be cooled, refrigerated overnight, and reheated slowly so the fat can be removed and the flavours deepen. The wine should be a drinkable Burgundy or a good Pinot Noir; thin cheap wine produces a thin cheap sauce.

recipeTools.notes: A large heavy casserole with a lid, oven-proof.

content.text: Brown the beef in batches with space between each piece: crowding the pan steams rather than browns the meat and leaves the stew looking grey. The browning step is what builds the deep flavour base of the finished dish. The whole process takes patience, but the preparation time is mostly hands-off oven time. Make this the day before it is needed: after refrigerating, lift the solidified fat from the surface before reheating. The sauce should be coating and glossy; if it is still thin after 3 hours, remove the beef and reduce the sauce on the hob.

items.preparation: a full bottle, Burgundy or good Pinot Noir

content.text: Heat the oven to 150 C / fan 130 C / gas 2. Render the lardons in a large heavy casserole over medium heat. Remove and set aside. Increase the heat to high. Dry the beef pieces with kitchen paper, season, and brown in batches in the lardon fat, adding oil as needed. Each piece should be deep brown on at least two sides. Remove each batch and set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Soften the shallots for 4 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree. Cook for 1 minute. Sprinkle over the flour and stir. Pour in the wine and stock, scraping up the brown bits from the base. Add the thyme, bay, lardons, and beef. Bring to a simmer. Cover and transfer to the oven.

Braise for 2 hours. Meanwhile, fry the mushrooms in butter over high heat until golden. After 2 hours, add the mushrooms to the casserole. Cook for a further 45 minutes to 1 hour until the beef is very tender. Season and scatter with parsley. Serve with mashed potato or buttered noodles.
